title: Simulation-Informed Diffusion for Decentralized Multi-robot Motion Planning
claim: A single model first simulates neighbors' futures, then plans under constraints, and triggers communication only when planning fails.
layout: 5 panels, left-to-right, colored background bands grouping stages, arrows between
description: Five square panels run left to right, labeled (a) Local Observation, (b) CADM as Simulator, (c) CADM as Planner, (d) Infeasible Planning and (e) Communication. Each panel is a top-down 2-D map. A blue robot sits at the center of a dashed observation circle, with a gray neighbor, beige square obstacles and star-shaped goals. Panel (a) shows the raw scene. Panel (b) adds a gray simulated neighbor trajectory, labeled w/ C_sim. Panel (c) adds the robot's blue planned trajectory, labeled w/ C_plan. Panel (d) shows the neighbor's simulated path crossing the robot's path, a red X and the note 'No feasible traj.'. Panel (e) shows the neighbor yielding, a green check, 'Resolved' and 'Go First'. Black solid arrows link (a) to (c). Dashed hollow arrows link (c) to (d) and (d) to (e). A light-blue band behind (b) and (c) marks 'Same CADM for simulation and planning'. A light-yellow band behind (d) and (e) marks 'Communication only when necessary'. The band titles are partly cropped at the top.
caption: Overview of SID. From a local observation, the robot uses CADM first to simulate feasible future trajectories for neighboring robots and then to plan its own trajectory under safety constraints. If the local planner cannot find a feasible trajectory under the current simulated constraints, SID triggers communication among the affected robots to coordinate actions.
abstract: Decentralized multi-robot motion planning requires each robot to generate collision-free trajectories from local observations, without global sensing or reliable communication. However, most existing planners, whether classical or learning-based, generate trajectories from a static snapshot of the local observation, which limits their ability to anticipate the future behavior of neighboring robots. This limitation is critical as the number of robots increases and the environment becomes more cluttered. Motivated by world models that use future state estimation to improve planning decisions, this paper introduces Simulation-Informed Diffusion (SID), a decentralized framework built on constraint-aware diffusion models (CADM) that simulate neighboring robots' future trajectories to guide each robot's own planning. SID first uses CADM to simulate the future trajectories of neighboring robots from their currently observed states, and then uses the same CADM to plan each robot's own trajectory under safety constraints informed by these simulations. Crucially, the accurate simulation of neighbors enables a minimal communication scheme that triggers coordination only when necessary in highly congested scenarios. Experiments across diverse environments show that SID consistently outperforms baseline methods in terms of planning effectiveness and constraint satisfaction, and scales to scenarios with 108 robots and 160 obstacles.
